word:lxx:L700076.explanation: Abisou is a personal name, rendered “Abisou” or “Avisu.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in genealogical material, but its precise identification depends on the surrounding names and passage. It should therefore be read as a person’s name, with the spelling preserved according to the chosen rendering.

word:lxx:L700098.explanation: The word means “abyss”: a deep, unfathomable place or depth. As a noun, it refers to depths that lie beyond ordinary human reach or measurement. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 44 times, including passages connected with the deep waters, the earth’s depths, and places hidden from human sight. Its central idea is profound depth—something vast, inaccessible, and beyond ordinary limits. The precise force in any verse depends on how the surrounding passage describes that depth.

word:lxx:L700115.explanation: Agallim is a proper name, referring to a specifically named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its exact identity is not further defined by the available lexical information. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 15:8. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what Agallim refers to in that passage; the name itself supplies identification, not a broader abstract meaning.

word:lxx:L700159.explanation: Hagios means holy. It describes people, convocations, objects, and places as holy.

word:lxx:L700223.explanation: Adama, also called Athama, is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs six times, all in six Old Testament verses, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Hosea. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in each passage cannot be described further; its established meaning here is the place-name “Adama; Athama.”

word:lxx:L700285.explanation: This noun refers to “ill-repute” or “disgrace”: a state in which a person’s name or standing is held in dishonor. It describes damaged public regard rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, at Sirach 3:11. The word’s basic meaning is therefore a condition of dishonor; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that condition is presented there.

word:lxx:L700357.explanation: This noun means “immortality”: life that does not end in death. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it appears seven times, all in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. It names the condition or hope of continuing life, rather than an action someone performs. The surrounding passage determines how the word applies in each occurrence, but its central meaning remains the state of being deathless or everlasting.

word:lxx:L700511.explanation: This LXX noun means “guilelessness”: a state of being free from deceit or crafty intent. It describes straightforward innocence rather than hidden schemes, and can characterize a person’s inner quality or conduct. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing in Job and Psalms. Its basic sense remains focused on sincerity and freedom from guile, while the precise emphasis in any verse depends on its surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L700528.explanation: This adjective describes something that is not to be swallowed. It presents the idea of an item that should remain undigested or not be taken down, rather than something suitable for consumption. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 20:18. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its direct definition, while the precise force of the description in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. It belongs to the Greek Old Testament vocabulary and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament word.

word:lxx:L700564.explanation: This noun describes “licentiousness” or “intemperance”: conduct marked by a lack of restraint and self-control. It points to behavior that is not properly held in check, rather than merely an isolated mistake. The word appears once in the Greek LXX collection, in 4 Maccabees 13:7. Since the verse text is not provided here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700609.explanation: This noun means “upper city,” referring to the elevated or fortified part of a city. It names a place rather than an action, person, or quality. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its meaning remains consistent as a geographical term. The surrounding verse determines which city is meant in each occurrence, but the word itself points to the city’s higher district or stronghold.

word:lxx:L700645.explanation: This word means “cock,” the male bird of the chicken. It is a noun naming that bird rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 5:23. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: it identifies a cock. The precise significance of its use in that verse must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L700797.explanation: Amethyst is the name of a precious stone. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun identifies the gemstone itself rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs three times, in Exodus 28:19, Exodus 36:19, and Ezekiel 28:13. These occurrences place the word among descriptions of valuable or beautiful stones, while its basic meaning remains the name of the gem. The word’s precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the stone’s setting or use.

word:lxx:L700977.explanation: This verb means “carry up”: to move or bring something upward. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular sentence depends on what is being carried and where it is being brought, but the central idea remains upward movement or conveyance. word:lxx:L701008.explanation: This adjective means “husbandless,” describing a woman who does not have a husband. It identifies a marital condition rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains clear: lacking a husband. It is not a general term for being alone; it specifically concerns a woman’s marital status.

word:lxx:L701031.explanation: Anapedao means to leap up or spring up.

word:lxx:L701112.explanation: This word means “manly,” describing the manner in which an action is carried out. As an adverb, it tells the reader that someone acts in a manly way rather than naming a person or object. Its meaning is concise and direct, so it should not automatically be expanded into a specific virtue, emotion, or kind of courage without the surrounding verse. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees.

word:lxx:L701282.explanation: This verb means “come eye to eye”: to meet another directly, face to face. Its focus is a personal encounter, not a general state or abstract condition. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 12:14. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central sense. The word presents one person meeting another directly and personally.

word:lxx:L701303.explanation: Anōphelēs means useless, describing what brings no profit.

word:lxx:L701479.explanation: This noun means “piercing”—the act or result of being pierced. It is a noun naming this action or result, rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Hosea 9:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s particular force in that passage must be understood from its context; its basic lexical sense remains “piercing.”

word:lxx:L701516.explanation: This Greek verb means to defend oneself or another, or to make a defense. It describes giving an answer or presenting a case when facing accusation, challenge, or opposition. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs three times, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central idea is a spoken or reasoned defense rather than a physical act of protection.

word:lxx:L701642.explanation: This verb means “faint”: to lose strength or become unable to continue normally. It describes the act or state of fainting rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:18. The word’s basic sense is therefore clear, while the precise force of that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, not on the word alone.

word:lxx:L701707.explanation: Argyrion means silver or money, and can refer to a silver piece. As money, it can be used to buy food.

word:lxx:L701790.explanation: This noun means “plowing,” the work of turning and preparing soil for cultivation. It names an agricultural activity rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 45:6. That single occurrence shows that the word belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of farming, but the reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text here to explain any further contextual emphasis. Its basic meaning remains the agricultural work of plowing the ground.

word:lxx:L702092.explanation: Atimazō means to dishonor, as when someone dishonors a parent or the helpless.

word:lxx:L702166.explanation: This adverb means “randomly” or “accidentally,” describing something done without a deliberate plan or fixed direction. It can express an action that happens by chance rather than through careful purpose. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense remains an action or event occurring unexpectedly or without intentional arrangement.

word:lxx:L702188.explanation: “Apharsachaioi; Afarsakhei” is a proper name used to identify a particular named group or people. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word with a general meaning, but as a designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezra: Ezra 5:6 and Ezra 6:6. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific identity and role of those named cannot be explained further here.

word:lxx:L702225.explanation: This adjective means “intolerable” or “insufferable”: it describes something that cannot be endured or borne. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:10. The word’s basic force is a strong negative judgment about the severity or burden of something, rather than a description of a person, action, or object by itself. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L702269.explanation: Achiezeri is a proper name, appearing in English as “Achiezeri” or “Akhiezeri.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:34. Because it is a name and no broader definition is supplied, its central meaning is the identification of the named person or entity associated with that occurrence. The exact role it carries in Numbers 26:34 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L702283.explanation: Achimi, also rendered Akhimi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament, and its role is simply to name that person. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 4:2. Without the verse text and surrounding genealogy, Scripture does not provide enough context here to say more about the person’s identity or significance.

word:lxx:L702337.explanation: Baalgad is a proper name, rendered as “Baalgad” or “Vaalgath.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 11:17 and Joshua 12:7. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in each passage cannot be described further, but its lexical meaning is the name itself.

word:lxx:L702548.explanation: This adjective describes someone as “grievous of tongue” or as “speaking a foreign language.” It points to speech that is difficult or burdensome in relation to the tongue, with the wording also covering a person who speaks another language. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 3:5. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical sense centers on difficult or unfamiliar speech.

word:lxx:L702571.explanation: Basellan, also rendered Vasellan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 21:30. Its precise identification and role depend on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L702610.explanation: This verb means “confirm”—to make something firm, certain, or established. It expresses the act of affirming or strengthening something so that it can be relied upon. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of recorded contexts. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the same: confirming or making secure what is being addressed.

word:lxx:L702687.explanation: This proper name identifies Bethel, also rendered “Vithil.” It is a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:32. The name itself does not provide the details of that passage’s setting or significance; those depend on the surrounding verse and context. Its lexical identity is therefore straightforward: it names Bethel, with Vithil given as an alternate rendering.

word:lxx:L702801.explanation: Bochori, also rendered Vokhori, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person connected with the events recorded in 2 Samuel 20. The name occurs eight times, all within that chapter. Its meaning is therefore primarily its use as a personal designation; the available information does not provide a separate definition or explain the name’s etymology.

word:lxx:L702838.explanation: This noun means “clod of earth,” referring to a lump or piece of soil. It names earth gathered into a distinct mass rather than loose dust or an abstract idea of land. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 7:5. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a physical clod of earth.

word:lxx:L702874.explanation: Gadalia is a proper name, also rendered Gathalia. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:18. The available wording supports recognizing it as a personal name, but does not provide a broader definition or meaning for the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703150.explanation: Godollathi is a personal name, also represented as Gothollathi, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper noun in the Greek LXX, it functions to identify an individual by name. It occurs twice in this corpus, both in 1 Chronicles: once in 25:4 and once in 25:29. The available information establishes the name’s identity and usage, but does not provide a further lexical meaning.

word:lxx:L703239.explanation: Dabōr, also written Thavor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:58. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a particular person or place named in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific reference. The form itself does not provide a broader abstract meaning.

word:lxx:L703275.explanation: This word is the proper name “Damaskos; Thamaskos,” used to identify a named location rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 44 times, including passages from Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Amos. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points readers to the same named place whenever it occurs in the LXX.

word:lxx:L703356.explanation: Denethi is a proper name, appearing as “Denethi; Thenethi.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, at 1 Chronicles 3:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise person or role identified by the name must be determined from that passage itself. The name should therefore be understood as a specific biblical designation, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

word:lxx:L703381.explanation: Dessaos, also rendered “Thessaos,” is a proper name identifying a person. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its meaning is tied to the individual who bears the name. This Greek LXX name occurs once, in the deuterocanonical book of 2 Maccabees, at 14:16. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the person’s role cannot be explained further here, but the lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal designation rather than a common noun or descriptive title.

word:lxx:L703406.explanation: This verb means to “give a public address”—to speak openly before a gathered audience. It describes public speaking rather than private conversation, and its emphasis is on addressing people directly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding passage determines the particular purpose or subject of the address, but the word itself focuses on the public act of speaking.

word:lxx:L703613.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “support.” It describes the action of supporting someone or something, rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across several books from Genesis through Proverbs. Its precise expression depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of support. The English rendering is not available here, so the clearest meaning is the stated sense “support.”

word:lxx:L703734.explanation: Dioti means because, connecting a statement with its reason.

word:lxx:L703778.explanation: This noun refers to an assayer or scrutineer—someone who examines or tests carefully. It describes a person whose role is to inspect something closely and determine its quality or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Jeremiah 6:27. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense remains a careful examiner or tester.

word:lxx:L703855.explanation: This noun means “unlucky day”: a day viewed as bringing bad fortune or unfavorable circumstances. It names the day itself rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a day considered unlucky.

word:lxx:L703972.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “lie in; wrapped up in.” It describes something being situated within or enclosed in something else, rather than standing apart from it. As a verb, it expresses a condition or position: something lies in a place or is wrapped up in it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, in Genesis and Esther. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L704036.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “sitting-place”: a place or seat connected with sitting. It names a location associated with sitting rather than an action or activity. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs six times across five verses, chiefly in 1 Samuel, with one occurrence in Deuteronomy. Its precise reference in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a place designated for sitting.

word:lxx:L704173.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to decide finally or settle a matter. It describes bringing an issue to a definite conclusion rather than leaving it unresolved. As a verb, it expresses an action—someone determines an outcome or establishes a settlement. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L704199.explanation: Ekthlibō means to squeeze out, as grapes are squeezed into a cup.

word:lxx:L704429.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Eleutheros” or “Eleftheros.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses. The exact person it identifies must be determined from the surrounding passage, since a name by itself does not describe that person’s role or significance.

word:lxx:L704465.explanation: Elibema, also rendered Elivema, is a proper name for a person. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs seven times, all within Genesis 36. The available references show repeated use of the same name in that genealogy, but the name itself does not describe the person’s character or role. Those details must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

word:lxx:L704560.explanation: Ememaon is a proper name preserved as “Ememaōn” or “Ememaon,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:28. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its underlying meaning. Its precise significance in Joshua therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L704667.explanation: Enatos is a proper name, rendered “Enatos.” It functions as a personal or named designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 23 times across 22 verses, from Leviticus through 2 Maccabees. The word appears in Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, but the available lexical information identifies its name rather than explaining a broader descriptive meaning. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L704762.explanation: This verb means to have something in one’s thoughts—to think about it or keep it in mind. In the Greek Old Testament translation and related Greek writings, it describes inward mental attention rather than an outward action. The word occurs seven times in this corpus, appearing in both Old Testament books and later Greek Jewish writings. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L704803.explanation: ἐντομίς means an “incision” or “gash”: a cut made into the body. It is a noun describing the cut itself rather than the act of cutting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in passages from Leviticus and Jeremiah. Its basic sense focuses on a bodily cut or wound. The surrounding verse determines how that cut functions in the passage, but the word itself names the physical incision or gash.

word:lxx:L705004.explanation: This Greek word means “beg”: to ask someone earnestly for help, provision, or something needed. It is a verb, so it describes the act of making such a request rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Psalms and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a direct appeal for what one lacks or desires.

word:lxx:L705048.explanation: The word means “lodge”: a place for staying. As a noun, it names the lodging place itself, not the act of staying or a person who stays there. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 37 times across 35 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for a place where people may stay. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L705071.explanation: This noun means “interrogation”: a deliberate process of questioning someone to obtain information or an explanation. It refers to more than a casual question, emphasizing directed inquiry. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 43:7. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of questioning or being questioned in a formal, purposeful way.

word:lxx:L705152.explanation: This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “in fit time”. It describes something suited to the right moment or occurring at an appropriate time, rather than being early, late, or poorly timed. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears four times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its meaning is focused and specific rather than broadly represented across many books. The surrounding verse determines what situation is being called timely.

word:lxx:L705310.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “cutting on the surface; incision”—a cut made into or across a surface. It names the act or result of making such a cut, rather than describing a person or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both in 2 Maccabees, appearing in 2 Maccabees 2:26 and 2:28. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a surface cut or incision.

word:lxx:L705387.explanation: This adjective means “arable”: land that is suitable for cultivation or farming. It describes ground in terms of its usefulness for growing crops, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 13:48–49. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its precise role in either passage, but its basic sense remains land capable of being worked for agricultural purposes.

word:lxx:L705592.explanation: This word means “fit,” describing something appropriate or well-suited for its intended use. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, thing, or circumstance as matching what is needed rather than being unsuitable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalms 31:6. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is suitability or proper matching.

word:lxx:L705637.explanation: This adjective describes something of good size—something very large. It points to notable physical magnitude rather than naming an action or feeling. In the Greek LXX, it appears twice, once in 1 Samuel and once in Baruch, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its basic sense remains straightforward: the person or thing described is impressively large or substantial. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself emphasizes size.

word:lxx:L705783.explanation: This adverb means “thereupon” or “immediately afterwards,” marking an action or event that follows another in sequence. It draws attention to what happens next, without by itself explaining the reason for that next event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning is a close temporal connection between two events.

word:lxx:L705905.explanation: This noun refers to the act of taking someone alive—capturing a person while they remain living. In the Greek Old Testament, or Septuagint, it occurs twice: in Numbers 21:35 and Deuteronomy 2:34. Its central idea is capture that preserves life, rather than describing death or destruction. These references show where the word appears, while the particular force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706049.explanation: This word refers to the number nine. It functions as an indeclinable number, meaning its form does not change for grammatical purposes. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalm 118:65. The supplied lexical definition identifies it simply as “9; teth,” so its meaning is numerical rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

word:lxx:L706140.explanation: This adverb describes something done “wonderfully” or “terribly,” emphasizing that it is extraordinary in either a marvelous or fearsome way. It modifies an action or description rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs four times, across Psalms, Daniel, and Sirach. The exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea is that something is strikingly beyond the ordinary.

word:lxx:L706232.explanation: This word means “sheath,” a covering or case used to hold and protect a blade. It is a noun naming that object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Exodus and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the object functions in that particular passage.

word:lxx:L706368.explanation: Iabnēl, also given as Iavnil, is a proper name: it identifies a distinct named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available lexical information preserves the name in these two forms but does not specify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:11, so its precise referent belongs to that passage’s surrounding context.

word:lxx:L706386.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Iaēl, also rendered Iel. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs six times in six verses, all within Judges 4–5, from Judges 4:17 through Judges 5:24. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, while the word itself functions simply as the person’s name.

word:lxx:L706401.explanation: This is the personal name Jacob, rendered in Greek as “Iakōb” or “Iakov.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 396 times, with its greatest concentration in Genesis, where Jacob is first named. The name also appears throughout later biblical books when referring to him or to his descendants. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706474.explanation: This noun means “ibis,” the name of a bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 34:11. The word identifies the creature itself rather than an action, quality, or relationship. Because the available information does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding context, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained here. Its basic meaning remains simple and definite: an ibis, a particular kind of bird.

word:lxx:L706553.explanation: Ieēla, also rendered Iila, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, in Ezra 2:56. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description, so it is best understood as the identifying name recorded in that passage.

word:lxx:L706746.explanation: This word refers to an Egyptian and Jewish liquid measure called a “hin.” It is a noun used for measuring liquids in Old Testament passages translated in the Greek Septuagint, especially in instructions concerning offerings, anointing oil, and other prescribed quantities.
